title: Anthony Albanese's government hires 28 public servants a day
text:
By NICHOLAS COMINO, POLITICAL REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

Published:  13:09 AEST, 31 August 2026   |  Updated:  13:15 AEST, 31 August 2026

109

View  comments

The Albanese government has hired a staggering 28 new public servants a day since taking office, with the federal workforce closing in on a record 200,000 employees.

Analysis by the Australian Financial Review of 103 federal agencies found 92 increased their staffing numbers between June 2022 and December 2025, driving a 23 per cent increase in the size of the Australian Public Service in just three and a half years.

Since Labor's election victory in May 2022, the federal public service has grown from 159,179 employees in June 2022 to 195,847 by December 2025, an increase of about 36,700 staff.

The growth follows one of the Albanese government's first major decisions to abolish a staffing cap imposed by the former Coalition government, which had limited the size of the public service to about 155,000 employees, roughly equivalent to 2007 levels.

The cap, introduced by former finance minister Mathias Cormann, had restricted the number of public servants agencies could directly employ.

Critics argued the policy encouraged departments to rely more heavily on external consultants and contractors, who were not included in the cap.

The government has defended the expansion, arguing the size of the public service remains broadly consistent with historic levels when measured against Australia's population.

Around 28 public servants have been added to the APS per day since Labor was elected

Budget papers released in May 2026 showed public servants accounted for about 0.7 per cent of Australia's 28 million people in December 2025.

That proportion was slightly lower than when the Howard government left office in 2007, when public servants made up about 0.75 per cent of Australia's 21 million population.

Labor has also argued that bringing work back into government departments has reduced reliance on consultants and contractors and rebuilt public sector capability.

The biggest increases were concentrated in a handful of agencies responsible for the government's largest and most complex programs.

The National Disability Insurance Agency recorded the biggest rise, adding 5,986 staff and more than doubling its workforce from 5,066 to 11,052 as the NDIS continued to expand.

Defence added 3,823 employees, growing its workforce to 20,710 as the government ramped up military capability and prepared for projects such as the AUKUS submarines.

The Department of Home Affairs grew by 2,753 employees to 16,611, reflecting greater demands across immigration, border protection and national security.

The Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water also saw significant growth, adding 2,420 employees as Labor pursued its climate and energy agenda, taking its workforce from 3,714 to 6,134.

Katy Gallagher (pictured) said the public service size 'about right' when asked in late 2025

Is the massive growth in Australia's public service delivering real value for taxpayers or just waste?

Meanwhile, Services Australia, which administers Centrelink, Medicare and other key government services, added 1,730 employees to reach 34,026, making it the largest agency in the Commonwealth public service.

Asked about the growth in public service numbers last November, Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said the federal workforce was now 'roughly the right size'.

Gallagher defended the increase, arguing that the additional staff were helping deliver 'improved service outcomes ... for the Australian people' and reducing the government's reliance on external consultants and contractors.
